s: The Good Principle is the world and order, source of Mazda’s good things. Good Spirit, Âtar, Keresâspa, Glory, Victory, and the Law defend it against Azi Dahâka and other fiends.
Holy religion, established worldwide and abundantly nourished, receives King Vîstâspa’s support to drive away the Drug and uphold Ahura and Zarathustra’s law.
The living world is an ever-living creation restored at Saoshyant’s wish; Astvat-ereta’s look delivers its creatures to immortality, after which it never ages, dies, decays, or rots.

comes_with life [during the restoration of the world] Immortality comes when the world is restored and the dead rise. Astvat-ereta's look will also deliver the whole of the living creatures to immortality.
is_a Yast The XX. Vanant Yast concerns sacrifice, prayer, propitiation, and glorification directed to the star Vanant.
Vanant is a holy star made by Mazda, master of holiness, invoked through sacrifice and prayer as strong and healing against Angra Mainyu’s accursed Khrafstras.
is_a accursed and most foul The Khrafstras are described as accursed and most foul, and Vanant is invoked to withstand them.

Praise of Holiness is a word of truth that glorifies Ahura Mazda, the waters, earth, cattle, plants, and all good things born of the good principle. Recited with full faith and a devoted heart, it praises these beings and things. Its value increases according to the moment of recitation, including eating, drinking Haoma, waking, sleeping, rising, dying, and cohabitation. In its greatest recital, worth all between earth and heavens, it renounces evil thoughts, words, and deeds.

A faithful person’s soul, a spiritual entity departing from the body, remains near the head for three nights. It sings the Ustavaiti Gâtha and tastes immense pleasure, while worshipping good waters and Âtar. At third-night dawn it meets a sweet-scented wind and its own conscience. It then progresses through Good-Thought, Good-Word, and Good-Deed Paradise to Endless Lights, and is guided along the ways to Garô-nmâna.
Karshvare Hvaniratha is a Karshvare with cattle and chariots but no men, matched in greatness, goodness, and fairness by a final recital praising Holiness.
is_a text unit Yast XXII describes the postmortem experiences of faithful and wicked people, their souls’ destinations, and related teachings from Ahura Mazda.

The faithful person worships Mazda and lives by good thoughts, words, deeds, and religion, supporting the Law through worship, sacrifice, and aid to the poor. After death, a beautiful conscience meets him; he crosses the Paradises and reaches Endless Light.

eats poison and poisonous stench [after perishing] The wicked person has evil thoughts, evil words, evil deeds, and evil religion. After death, the wicked person receives poison and poisonous stench as food.

A wicked person’s soul remains near the skull for three nights after death, singing the Kima Gâtha and tasting suffering. At third-night dawn it encounters snow, stench, and a foul northern wind, then successively enters Evil-Thought Hell, Evil-Word Hell, Evil-Deed Hell, and Endless Darkness.

l: world of the spirit, Yashts (Yasts) XIII-XXIV
s: The world of the spirit is contrasted with the material world and is described as undecaying.
The Good-Thought Paradise is where the faithful person’s soul arrives after its first step.

Good-Word Paradise is the second destination reached by a faithful soul after death, following Good Thoughts and preceding Good Deeds, as part of a progression toward Endless Light and the Garô-nmâna of Ahura Mazda.
The Good-Deed Paradise is where the faithful person’s soul arrives after its third step.
The Evil-Thought Hell is where the wicked person’s soul is laid after its first step.
The Evil-Word Hell is where the wicked person’s soul is laid after its second step.
The Evil-Deed Hell is where the wicked person’s soul is laid after its third step.
The Endless Darkness is where the wicked person’s soul is laid after its fourth step.
leads_to world of the spirit [from the material world] After the faithful person’s death, the soul remains near the head for three nights, then travels through paradises to the Endless Lights.
leads_to world of the spirit [from the material world] After the wicked person’s death, the soul remains near the skull for three nights, then travels through hells to the Endless Darkness.

At the third-night dawn, the faithful person’s soul experiences plants, scents, and a sweet-scented southern wind, while the wicked person’s soul experiences snow, stench, and a foul-scented northern wind.
On the third night, the faithful person’s soul remains near the head in pleasure, while the wicked person’s soul remains near the skull in suffering.

l: good thoughts, good words, and good deeds, Yashts (Yasts) XIII-XXIV
s: Good thoughts, good words, and good deeds characterize the faithful person and determine the successive paradises reached by the faithful person’s soul.

l: evil thoughts, evil words, and evil deeds, Yashts (Yasts) XIII-XXIV
s: Evil thoughts, evil words, and evil deeds characterize the wicked person and determine the successive hells reached by the wicked person’s soul.

A blessing for king Vîstâspa wishes him to resemble exemplary figures in many virtues and powers, including beneficence, strength, truth, welfare, and freedom from sickness and death; it concludes by wishing fulfillment and passage to the holy Ones’ bright, blissful abode.
is_a bridge [powerful and well-kept] The Kinvat-bridge is a powerful, well-kept bridge known afar and kept by virtue. The soul of man crosses it in the joy of perfect holiness.

is_a worshipper of Mazda [recipient of food and support] A priest should be treated like the brightest offspring of one's own blood and should not be bad or unfriendly. A sacrifice offered through bad or unfriendly priests is treated as though no sacrifice had been offered to the Amesha-Spentas.

The document comprises five Nyâyis hymns and prayers centered on Ahura Mazda and sacred beings. The Khôrshêd Nyâyis honors the Sun, Mithra, Tistrya, and Ahura Mazda, affirms good thoughts, words, and deeds, rejects evil, repeats Ashem Vohû, and identifies the worshipper as Zarathustra’s follower. The Mihir Nyâyis offers prayer to Ahura Mazda, the Amesha-Spentas, Fravashis, Vayu, and especially Mithra, portrayed as powerful, vigilant, truthful, and lord of wide pastures and countries. The Mâh Nyâyis praises the Moon, the Bull, Waters, healing and glorious gods, seeking strength, victory, welfare, children, brightness, glory, and a blissful abode. The Âbân Nyâyis recounts Ahura Mazda directing Spitama Zarathustra to sacrifice to Ardvi Sûra Anâhita, the holy water-spring whose river serves the seven Karshvares and purifies seed and wombs. Finally, the Âtas Nyâyis venerates Âtar, Ahura Mazda’s son, requesting welfare, knowledge, courage, offspring, prosperity, and fellowship with the holy Ones for proper worshippers.

Ahura Mazda is a Lord honored by a person offering sacrifice in invocation. Hailed before all creatures, he is invoked with the Amesha-Spentas, Mithra, and the Sun, which is described as his two eyes. He made Mithra most glorious among heavenly gods; his will is the law of holiness. As source of Âtar, his glory, beneficence, and works are praised, while worshippers seek his rejoicing, perfect piety, and strength.
The Sun, swift-horsed, bright, undying, and shining, receives sacrifices and honor as aligned with the Amesha-Spentas and one of Ahura Mazda’s two eyes.

The Amesha-Spentas are holy beings hailed as one with the Sun. Invocations offer them prayers, sacrifice, and the worshipper’s thoughts, words, deeds, heart, and life; prayer is asked to come to them.
A prayer declaring and praising holiness as the best of all good, teaching its association with perfection from its identification through its recitation.

Mithra is a lord of wide pastures and all countries, a truth-speaking chief in assemblies, powerful, well-shapen, strong, watchful, sleepless, and ever awake, with a thousand ears, ten thousand eyes, and full knowledge. Ahura Mazda made him most glorious among heavenly gods. He is hailed and invoked with Ahura Mazda for help and ease, while sacrifices and libations are offered to him.
Spitama Zarathustra, a holy man with a Fravashi, is hailed by worshippers who follow him; Ahura Mazda addresses him, instructing sacrifice, full worship, and advising those who appeal.

comes_to_an_end end [when Spenta Mainyu is addressed] The world is described as eventually coming to an end. The unit asks for the highest luminous space when that occurs and refers to holy gods of the world unseen.
Tistrya is a bright, glorious star with sound sight, honored through sacrifices offered to him and his rains.

The prayer is directed to Ahura Mazda, the Amesha-Spentas, the Fravashis of the holy Ones, and Vayu. It praises good thoughts, words, and deeds and seeks health, holiness, brightness, glory, and a blissful abode.

Sacrifice is offered to the Amesha-Spentas, Mithra, Ahura Mazda, the Sun, Tistrya, the holy gods, the stars, the moon, and other sacred beings. Libations are offered to Mithra, and the strength and vigour of Mithra are blessed.
The Moon, associated with Mithra and the Bull, keeps the only-created Bull’s seed, is hailed and watched, waxes and wanes, and receives sacrifices for brightness and glory.

Ahura Mazda, a lord, wills holiness as law, makes good waters and plants, and brings Ardvi Sûra Anâhita’s river down to increase settlements; he is praised and tells Spitama Zarathustra to sacrifice to her.

Ardvi Sûra Anâhita is a holy water-spring, a large river, and a master of holiness. Her good waters flow over the seven Karshvares; when she runs to sea Vouru-Kasha, she boils over its shores and middle. She makes males’ seed and females’ wombs pure and increases house, borough, town, and country. Sacrifice is offered for her brightness and glory, with libations, Haoma, meat, baresma, wisdom of the tongue, holy spells, words, and deeds. Most fully worshipped, she gives boons to one who hears specified prayers and makes the good waters pure.

l: Âtar, the son of Ahura Mazda, Nyayish
s: Âtar, the son of Ahura Mazda, receives sacrifice, prayer, propitiation, glorification, sacred wood, incense, food, fuel, and other offerings. He is described as beneficent, a warrior, a full source of glory and healing, and as dwelling with all Âtars alongside Nairyô-sangha in the navel of kings. He watches what passers-by bring and blesses those who offer properly prepared wood, granting them growing herds, sons, mastery of their vows, and joy of soul.
